name: Greens powders (AG1)

lead: Greens powders are blends of vegetables, algae, herbs, vitamins and minerals mixed into water as a daily drink. AG1 is the best-known brand, with roughly 75 ingredients, and users credit it for healthier-looking skin, steadier digestion and energy.

The chain people describe is broad micronutrient and plant intake, better nutrition and gut health, then a visible skin and energy payoff. Supporting trials are small and focus on nutrient status, and no studies were found on appearance outcomes.

paras: People mix a scoop into water once a day, usually in the morning, as an all-in-one add-on to their regular diet. AG1 is sold by subscription, often promoted through podcasts and influencers, and users commonly describe a few weeks before judging it.
No specific harms are described in the sources used here. Reported issues are cost, about US$79 per month in 2024, and proprietary-blend labelling that keeps some ingredient amounts undisclosed.

chain: Claimed better nutrition and gut health
angle.text: Greens powders such as AG1 are taken as a daily all-in-one supplement, with users crediting them for better skin, digestion and energy. The idea is a broad mix of vitamins, greens and herbs improving nutrition and gut health. Brand-supported trials are small and focus on nutrient status.

lead: Greens powders are powdered blends of vegetables, algae, herbs, vitamins and minerals mixed into water as a daily supplement. The best-known brand is AG1, formerly Athletic Greens, a Nevada-based company founded in December 2010 by Chris Ashenden that sells a roughly 75-ingredient powder by subscription [1].

AG1 is marketed heavily through podcasts and influencers, with creators paid through affiliate arrangements [1]. Critics quoted in coverage, including a Harvard Medical School professor, have described the supporting trials as very small, and have questioned the value of a many-ingredient blend [1].

paras: The company began with one product sold directly to consumers by subscription; its formula was changed more than 50 times between 2010 and 2024. It rebranded as AG1 in December 2021 after hiring Kat Cole as president and COO. Reported revenue rose from about US$160 million in 2021 to about US$600 million in 2024, and the company was valued at US$1.2 billion in January 2025 [1].
Ashenden resigned in 2024 after earlier criminal convictions in New Zealand became public, and Cole became CEO [1].

Podcasters including Tim Ferriss were early promoters, and Ferriss later became an investor; other celebrity investors and partners are listed in coverage [1]. JoAnn Manson of Harvard Medical School called the company's supporting trials very small, dietitian Charlotte Martin argues that so many ingredients make the amount of any single nutrient small, and Jonathan Jarry of McGill University says the blend has little scientific backing relative to its cost. Critics also note that some ingredient amounts are hidden within proprietary blends [1].
No studies found examining greens powders for appearance outcomes. Commentators describe the company's own supporting trials as small [1].

timeline.event: Athletic Greens founded by Chris Ashenden. [1]
Rebrands as AG1; Kat Cole joins as president and COO. [1]
